result: Chlamydomonas reinhardtii is a biflagellated freshwater green alga with features of both animal and plant cells, including motile flagella with stable MT bundles and dynamic cortical MTs that serve as tracks for cell wall enzyme delivery.
evaluation: Claims C1-C5 are well-supported by citations to established literature (Merchant et al., 2007; Paredez et al., 2006) and represent accepted knowledge about Chlamydomonas cellular organization. These are background claims establishing the model organism's characteristics.

result: Chlamydomonas flagella sever readily in response to environmental changes, particularly pH shock, where organic acid diffuses across the membrane, becomes ionized, triggers Ca2+ influx, and causes flagellar amputation and cortical MT changes within 5 minutes.
evaluation: Claims C6-C10 are supported by multiple citations (Lefebvre et al., 1978; Quarmby, 1996, 2009; Wheeler et al., 2008; Hilton et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2013) describing the well-characterized pH shock response. These represent established prior work on Chlamydomonas stress responses.

result: Autofluorescence from chloroplast photosynthetic pigments obscures commonly used fluorescent reporters in Chlamydomonas, but NeonGreen (NG), which is 2.7X brighter than EGFP, overcomes this limitation when used with EB1 as a carrier.
evaluation: Claims C11-C12 are supported by citations (Lang et al., 1991; Rasala et al., 2013; Shaner et al., 2013; Harris et al., 2016). The brightness advantage of NeonGreen is established in the literature, and its successful application to Chlamydomonas is documented.

result: EB1 is a central eukaryotic protein with an N-terminal domain that binds MT plus ends and a C-terminal domain that associates with various proteins. The two domains work together to accelerate MT dynamics and recruit +TIP effector proteins. Fluorescent EB1 exhibits a comet pattern in live imaging and is commonly used to report growing MTs, though binding to the GDP zone can increase in certain scenarios.
evaluation: Claims C13-C20 are well-supported by extensive citations (Su et al., 1995; Akhmanova and Steinmetz, 2010; Kumar and Wittmann, 2012; Rogers et al., 2002; Vitre et al., 2008; Maurer et al., 2012, 2014; Zanic et al., 2009; Gardner et al., 2013; Piehl et al., 2004; Matov et al., 2010; Tirnauer et al., 2002; Goldspink et al., 2013; Tortosa et al., 2013; Sayas and Ávila, 2014). These represent established knowledge about EB1 function.

result: Flagellated Chlamydomonas cells in interphase contain two mature basal bodies (BBs) and two probasal bodies, with each mature BB nucleating an axoneme. Four rootlet MT bundles arrange in a cruciate pattern, while cortical MTs are singular and highly dynamic. EB1-NG expressed at endogenous levels reveals dynamic cortical MTs as comets emerging from BBs and traveling toward the posterior pole.
evaluation: Claims C21-C32 are supported by citations (Dutcher and O'Toole, 2016; Mittelmeier et al., 2011; Picariello et al., 2014; Horst et al., 1999; Harris et al., 2016; Pedersen et al., 2003) and by Figure 1a-b showing the cellular organization and EB1-NG comet patterns. The data and prior literature converge to support these structural and dynamic features.

result: EB1-NG comets travel along the cell body contour toward the posterior pole where they vanish. Line scans show typical EB1 comet features with the brightest spot at the transitional state. MT growth rates vary nearly two-fold, with significantly different average velocities in TAP medium (5.8±0.26 μm/sec) versus Na+/HEPES (7.9±0.42 μm/sec, p<0.001), both within the normal range for eukaryotic cells.
evaluation: Claims C33-C40 are supported by quantitative data in Figure 1b-e, including line scans (C36), velocity distributions (C37-C38), and statistical analysis (C39). The Mann-Whitney U test with p<0.001 provides strong statistical support for the difference between conditions. The comparison to literature values (Harris et al., 2016) validates the measurements.

result: In long recordings, comets spontaneously switched to a bird cage-like pattern revealing all cortical MTs, then returned after ~1 min. In flattened cells, comets disappeared after ~100 s of illumination but returned after 30 s in darkness. Alternating light and dark periods replicated this reversible disappearance, suggesting that excitation illumination creates unfavorable conditions for MT dynamics that are reversed in darkness.
evaluation: Claims C41-C48 are supported by Figure 1f1-f2 and Videos 2-3 showing the reversible transitions between comet and bird cage patterns. The temporal dynamics are documented (C42, C45-C47), and the inference about light sensitivity (C48) is reasonable given the reproducible light/dark effects. However, the mechanism remains speculative.

result: The authors hypothesize that illumination opens channelrhodopsins that conduct cations and Cl-, and that changes in electrolyte concentrations modulate the MT system in Chlamydomonas.
evaluation: Claim C49 is supported by citations (Nagel et al., 2002, 2003; Hegemann and Berthold, 2009) about channelrhodopsin function. However, C50 is explicitly stated as a hypothesis. While the light-induced MT changes are documented (C41-C48), the causal link to electrolyte changes via channelrhodopsins requires direct testing.

result: Following injection of 20 mM HA/TAP in a perfusion chamber, all comets vanished within ~90 s. After washing with pH7 HEPES, comets re-appeared at the BB area within ~45 s and MT dynamics resumed, indicating that HA exposure causes disappearance of EB patterns by perturbing EB-MT interactions or causing cortical MTs to pause/disassemble, with rapid reformation after HA removal.
evaluation: Claims C51-C54 are supported by Figure 2b showing the temporal sequence of comet disappearance and recovery. The timing is documented (~90 s for disappearance, ~45 s for recovery), and the inference about mechanism (C53) is reasonable though not definitively proven. The rapid reversibility is clearly demonstrated.

result: In diffusion chambers with gradual acidification, a broken bird cage pattern with MTs and comets appeared before disappearance. Some MTs underwent endwise resorption with initial shortening speeds of 8 and 13 μm/min that decelerated toward BBs. These speeds are consistent with cortical MT shortening in tobacco cells (10±3 μm/min), faster than kinesin-13-catalyzed shortening, and slower than maximal shortening of purified tubulins (30 μm/min).
evaluation: Claims C55-C60 are supported by Figure 2c-d showing the bird cage pattern, endwise resorption, and kymograph measurements. The measured shortening speeds (C57) are compared to literature values with appropriate citations (Dixit and Cyr, 2004; Helenius et al., 2006; O'Brien et al., 1997), providing context for the observations.

result: In cells with EB1 signals in both cell body and flagella, comets vanished first before flagellar amputation, with static EB1 signals remaining at BBs. Deflagellation in diffusion chambers takes over one minute due to gradual acidification. The sequential events (increased shank binding, comet disappearance, endwise resorption, flagellar amputation) do not require TAP media components.
evaluation: Claims C61-C65 are supported by Figure 2e showing the temporal sequence and by comparison with perfusion data (Wheeler et al., 2008). The observation that events occur in different media (C65) is supported by experiments in both TAP and HEPES buffers. The sequential nature of events is well-documented.

result: To test whether HA-induced changes are due to H+ or Ca2+, cells were exposed to elevated extracellular Ca2+. At 30 mM Ca2+/HEPES, flagella remained attached and comet activity was robust, but at 75 mM Ca2+/HEPES, cells shed flagella and comets disappeared with static EB1 signals at BBs. The outcomes at high [Ca2+]ex and ≥20 mM HA are similar.
evaluation: Claims C66-C71 are supported by Figure 2g showing concentration-dependent Ca2+ effects and by citations (Weisenberg, 1972; O'Brien et al., 1997; Wheeler et al., 2008). The comparison between Ca2+ and HA effects (C71) is reasonable given the similar phenotypes at high concentrations, though the underlying mechanisms may differ.

result: WT cells in 5 mM HA exhibited a dynamic bird cage pattern with motile flagella and MTs that shrink or grow with comets. At 7.5 mM HA, only a few resorbing MTs were captured. At 10 mM HA, all MT patterns and comets disappeared. This concentration-dependent response indicates that low [HA] increases EB1 shank-binding (bird cage pattern), while higher concentrations stop MT growth and eliminate comets.
evaluation: Claims C72-C76 are supported by Figure 3a and Video 4 showing concentration-dependent effects. The progression from dynamic bird cage (5 mM) to few resorbing MTs (7.5 mM) to complete disappearance (10 mM) is clearly documented. The inference about mechanism (C75-C76) is reasonable given the dose-response relationship.

result: The tub2 β-tubulin mutant with more stable MTs showed normal comet patterns under control conditions but formed a stable bird cage pattern immediately after 10 mM HA exposure. HA-induced diminished EB1-NG signals in WT cells are not due to reduced NG brightness at low pH. In ~5 mM HA, EB1 dissociation from MT plus ends is inhibited (bird cage pattern), while higher HA concentrations block MT elongation and accelerate depolymerization, which is prevented by increased MT stability in tub2.
evaluation: Claims C77-C83 are supported by Figure 3b showing tub2 responses and by citations (Schibler and Huang, 1991; Shaner et al., 2013). The genetic approach using tub2 provides strong evidence that MT stability affects HA responses. The persistence of EB1-NG signal in tub2 at 10 mM HA (C81) rules out pH-dependent fluorescence loss as the primary mechanism.

result: Chelation of Ca2+ by pretreatment with 10 mM EGTA did not prevent HA-induced changes, whereas pH3 10 mM HCl did not elicit any responses. This indicates that HA-elicited changes in cortical MTs are due to intracellular rather than extracellular acidification and do not require extracellular Ca2+.
evaluation: Claims C84-C87 are supported by experimental data showing that EGTA pretreatment does not block HA effects while HCl (which cannot permeate membranes) has no effect. This provides strong evidence for the intracellular acidification mechanism (C86) and rules out a requirement for extracellular Ca2+ (C87).

result: Chlamydomonas expresses Na+/H+ exchangers and various channels and pumps at different locations to maintain electrolyte homeostasis.
evaluation: Claims C88-C89 are supported by citations (Pittman et al., 2009; Fujiu et al., 2011; Taylor et al., 2012) documenting the presence of these ion transport systems. This provides context for understanding how cells might respond to and recover from electrolyte perturbations.

result: After 5 min HA bath and wash with Na+/HEPES, dynamic EB1 signals emerged at BBs after ~50 s, but nascent MTs were thicker, fewer, and nearly uniformly decorated without typical comets. MT growth decelerated over time (60-159 s) and stopped by 180 s. Some static fibers split or had multiple comets in tandem, suggesting abnormal MTs with propensity for ectopic nucleation, branching, or bundling. These MTs were fewer, thicker, shorter, brighter, and longer-lived than the transient bird cage pattern.
evaluation: Claims C90-C101 are supported by Figure 4a-c and Video 5 showing the temporal progression and abnormal MT characteristics. The kymograph analysis (C98-C100) documents the deceleration and eventual cessation of growth. The inference about abnormal MT properties (C97, C101) is reasonable given the unusual morphology and dynamics, though the specific mechanisms remain speculative.

result: Thick static MTs formed after HA bath and wash are cold-resistant, remaining visible after 3 min on ice, while control MTs without HA treatment are cold-labile and initially undetectable after cold treatment. Dynamic EB1 signals gradually re-emerged at BBs after 30 s in controls. Comet activity was vibrant 55 min post-wash in HA-treated cells, indicating reversibility.
evaluation: Claims C102-C105 are supported by Figure 4d-e showing cold stability of post-HA MTs versus cold lability of control MTs. The cold resistance test provides strong evidence for altered MT stability. The recovery of normal dynamics after 55 min (C105) demonstrates that the changes are reversible, not permanent damage.

result: In tub2 cells, the frozen bird cage pattern remained after 5 min HA bath. After wash, comets returned and lengthened but appeared at the plus ends of existing MTs rather than at BBs, with the bird cage pattern gradually fading. This indicates that 10 mM HA cannot elicit resorption of more stable MTs in tub2, and comets preferentially return to old MTs which need to resorb to make room for new ones.
evaluation: Claims C106-C111 are supported by Figure 5a and Video 6 showing distinct recovery patterns in tub2 versus WT. The observation that comets appear on existing MTs rather than at BBs (C108) is clearly documented. The inference about MT stability preventing resorption (C110) is well-supported by the genetic evidence, though the speculation about MT turnover (C111) is less certain.

result: EB1-decorated MT fibers formed after HA bath only if the wash solution contained Na+ (NaOH-buffered HEPES or NaCl in ddw). Comets resumed profusely if the wash solution lacked Na+ (KOH-buffered HEPES, KCl, or ddw). Therefore, Na+ accounts for the reformation of thick, long-lived static MTs in the recovery phase.
evaluation: Claims C112-C114 are strongly supported by Figure 6a showing the differential effects of Na+-containing versus Na+-free wash solutions. The clear dichotomy between Na+ (thick MTs) and K+ (comets) provides compelling evidence that Na+ specifically drives the formation of abnormal static MTs. This is a key mechanistic finding.

result: Thick MTs formed in cells resuspended in 21 mM Na+/EGTA, growing after 5 min but static after 10 min. In contrast, cells in 21 mM K+/EGTA had vibrant comet activities but quickly burst, indicating perturbed plasma membrane.
evaluation: Claims C115-C118 are supported by Figure 6b showing time-dependent effects of Na+/EGTA versus K+/EGTA. The EGTA treatment presumably permeabilizes membranes, allowing direct testing of intracellular ion effects. The cell bursting in K+/EGTA (C118) indicates membrane damage, which complicates interpretation but doesn't invalidate the Na+ effects.

result: At 55 mM NaCl in HEPES, MTs were still growing but with longer comets showing modest tapering of intensity. The average velocity was significantly different from 5 mM Na+ (p=0.0497, <0.05), indicating that high [Na+]ex can raise [Na+]in, increasing the time EB1 spent at plus ends and thus comet lengths. MT growth is sensitive to [Na+] but less than EB1 plus end binding.
evaluation: Claims C119-C122 are supported by Figure 6c showing longer comets, linescan analysis, velocity distributions, and statistical comparison. The p-value of 0.0497 is marginally significant (just below 0.05), indicating a modest effect on growth rate. The inference about differential sensitivity (C122) is reasonable given that comet length changes are more pronounced than velocity changes.

result: At 150-200 mM [Na+]ex for 5 min, flagellar motility ceased and comets vanished in most cells, though static EB1 signals remained at BBs. The algal MT system undergoes a range of changes as a function of [Na+].
evaluation: Claims C123-C125 are supported by Figure 6d showing high Na+ effects. The dose-response relationship across multiple Na+ concentrations (C125) is well-documented throughout Figures 6-7. The similar phenotype to high Ca2+ and HA suggests a common mechanism at high concentrations, possibly hypertonicity.

result: Frozen thick MTs caused by 21 mM Na+/EGTA or 5 mM Na+/HEPES wash after HA bath may be triggered by less than 21 mM [Na+]in due to passive diffusion or H+/Na+ exchange. [Na+]in is likely even lower in cells exposed to 55 mM [Na+]ex with long comets and growing MTs. Few or no EB1-decorated MTs at 150-200 mM [Na+]ex or 75 mM [Ca2+]ex suggest MT disassembly at hypertonic concentrations.
evaluation: Claims C126-C128 involve inferences about intracellular ion concentrations without direct measurements. While the reasoning is plausible based on permeability and transport mechanisms, the actual [Na+]in values are not measured. The speculation about hypertonicity (C128) is reasonable but not definitively proven. Direct measurement of intracellular ion concentrations would strengthen these claims.

result: Salt stress triggers responses in Chlamydomonas including inhibited multiplication. In synchronized cultures, mother cells undergo 1-3 rounds of division during the dark period forming sporangia. Sporangia ratios were inversely related to NaCl concentrations, with delayed peak formation at 100 mM and no sporangia at 200 mM. No comets or EB1-decorated MTs were observed at 200 mM NaCl.
evaluation: Claims C129-C135 are supported by Figure 7a-b showing sporangia formation data and fluorescence imaging. The inverse relationship between NaCl and cell division (C132-C134) is clearly documented with quantitative data. The correlation with absence of MT dynamics at 200 mM (C135) links MT disruption to proliferation defects.

result: Comets lengthened in 55 and 100 mM Na+/TAP with similar lengthening degrees. Mean comet speeds at 55 mM (8.38±0.345 μm/min) and 100 mM (7.79±0.628 μm/min) were not significantly different (p=0.385) but were faster than 0 mM (6.41±0.241 μm/min, p<0.001 for 0 vs 55 mM; p=0.05 for 0 vs 100 mM).
evaluation: Claims C136-C138 are supported by Figure 7c showing linescan analysis and statistical comparisons. The statistical tests are appropriate (t-test and Mann-Whitney U test), and the p-values are clearly reported. The finding that 55 and 100 mM have similar effects on comet length and speed is well-documented.

result: Absence of comets and decorated MTs is consistent with blocked proliferation at 200 mM NaCl. However, the similar comet lengths and speeds for 55 and 100 mM NaCl do not correlate with differences in dividing cell numbers and delay.
evaluation: Claims C139-C140 are supported by comparing Figure 7a (proliferation) with Figure 7b-c (MT dynamics). The correlation at 200 mM (C139) is clear, but the lack of correlation at intermediate concentrations (C140) suggests that MT dynamics alone do not fully explain proliferation differences, indicating additional factors are involved.

result: The changes in algal MT system elicited by intracellular acidification are swift, stunning, and novel. The bird cage pattern of shank binding is the most sensitive response, reliably elicited by 5 mM HA. Extracellular Ca2+ is not required for HA-induced changes since they occur after K+/EGTA treatment.
evaluation: Claims C141-C143 summarize key findings supported by Figures 2-3. The characterization as "swift, stunning, and novel" (C141) is subjective but justified by the rapid and reversible nature of the responses. The sensitivity of the bird cage pattern (C142) is documented in Figure 3a. The Ca2+ independence (C143) is supported by EGTA experiments.

result: The intracellular pH resulting from [HA]ex that triggers MT changes is expected to be higher than 6.3, based on: (1) changes appearing before deflagellation at pH 6.3, (2) swiftness and reversibility inconsistent with apoptotic pathways (induced by 0.3-0.4 pH unit drop from normal 6.8), and (3) transient triggering by illumination. A slight imbalance of pH homeostasis is sufficient to elicit immediate MT changes.
evaluation: Claims C144-C148 present a logical argument supported by multiple lines of evidence: temporal sequence (C145, Figure 2e), comparison with apoptosis thresholds (C146-C147, citations provided), and light-induced effects (Figure 1f). The inference about pH range (C144) is reasonable though not directly measured. The conclusion about pH sensitivity (C148) is well-supported.

result: The pI values of Chlamydomonas α-tubulin (5.01), β-tubulin (4.82), and EB1 (5.7) suggest that pH decreases will make these proteins less negatively charged, especially at C-terminal acidic tails. The resulting decreased repulsion could explain increased EB1 affinity to GDP-tubulin (bird cage pattern). Further pH decreases may inhibit MT growth and EB1 binding to plus ends (comet disappearance).
evaluation: Claim C149 provides pI values that appear to be calculated or obtained from databases. Claims C150-C152 present a mechanistic hypothesis based on electrostatic principles. While the reasoning is chemically sound and consistent with observations, it remains speculative without direct biochemical evidence of pH-dependent binding changes. The hypothesis is plausible but requires experimental validation.

result: The responses elicited by slight increases in [Na+]in and [H+]in are distinct in pattern and pace. The slower pace of Na+-induced responses is likely due to low Na+ permeability compared to K+. The direct switch from lengthening comets to MT resorption suggests NaCl alone cannot raise [Na+]in incrementally. Continual changes over 10 min in 21 mM Na+/EGTA indicate effects occur before [Na+]in reaches 21 mM. Similar responses emerge faster (45-180 s) after HA bath with 5 mM Na+ wash, suggesting accelerated [Na+]in rise via Na+/H+ exchangers.
evaluation: Claims C153-C158 present a coherent mechanistic model supported by multiple experiments (Figures 4-6). The comparison of H+ versus Na+ kinetics (C153-C154) is supported by the data. The citation about Na+ permeability (C155, Ronkin and Buretz, 1960) provides context. The inferences about [Na+]in dynamics (C156-C158) are reasonable though not directly measured, and the role of Na+/H+ exchangers (C158, Pittman et al., 2009) is plausible.

result: Based on incremented rather than all-or-none responses, the algal MT system changes as a function of [Na+]in. Raising [K+]ex had no evident effect, which is reasonable given high [K+]in (~70 mM). This selective sensitivity to Na+ rules out mere ionic effects. One possibility is that Na+ binds to particular sites in algal tubulins, analogous to Ca2+ binding sites in mammalian tubulins.
evaluation: Claims C159-C163 are supported by the dose-response data throughout Figures 6-7. The lack of K+ effect (C160) is shown in Figure 6a. The [K+]in value (C161, Malhotra and Glass, 1995) provides context. The inference about ion specificity (C162) is well-supported. The speculation about Na+ binding sites (C163) is plausible given the analogy to Ca2+ (Solomon, 1977; Serrano et al., 1986) but remains hypothetical.

result: EB1 signals largely vanish at ≥150 mM [Na+]ex, similar to 10 mM HA and 75 mM [Ca2+]ex, except for residual static signals at BBs. These changes likely reflect simultaneous disassembly, paused growth, and immobile EB1 at BBs. The similar outcomes with distinct ions and cell shrinkage at higher concentrations suggest hypertonicity is involved. High concentration responses could result from one cation exceeding a threshold or concurrent rises of multiple electrolytes as H2O moves out. The capture of endwise resorption only at low concentrations suggests increased ion concentrations heighten shortening incidence and/or speed.
evaluation: Claims C164-C168 synthesize observations across multiple experiments (Figures 2g, 6d, 7b). The comparison of different ions (C164) is well-documented. The inference about mechanisms (C165) is supported by citations (Yan et al., 2006; Pedersen et al., 2003). The hypertonicity hypothesis (C166-C167) is reasonable given cell shrinkage and similar effects with different ions, though not definitively proven. The observation about resorption (C168) is supported by Figures 2d and 3a.

result: Ca2+ blocks MT formation, while 0.5-0.6 mM Ca2+ can increase shortening incidence and accelerate shortening speed beyond 150 μm/min in vitro. Although pH shock and high [Ca2+]ex only temporarily raise [Ca2+]in to 1 μM, this may suffice to accelerate shortening. Some electrolyte-elicited changes could be evoked by signaling pathways that occur later, slower, and last longer than direct effects. Examples include kinesin-13 phosphorylation for >20 min after pH shock, activation of tubulin-kinase and phospholipase D by osmotic/salt stress in plants, and MAP kinase involvement in yeast recovery from sorbitol hypertonicity.
evaluation: Claims C169-C174 are well-supported by extensive citations documenting Ca2+ effects on MTs (Weisenberg, 1972; Karr et al., 1980; O'Brien et al., 1997), Ca2+ dynamics (Wheeler et al., 2008), and signaling pathways in various organisms (Wang et al., 2013; Perrineau et al., 2014; Khona et al., 2016; Fujita et al., 2013; Dhonukshe et al., 2003; Robertson and Hagan, 2008). These provide important context for interpreting the rapid direct effects versus potential slower signaling responses.

result: The electrolyte sensitivity of algal MT system contrasts with the perceived stable MT system in interphase mammalian cells (140 mM [Na+]ex, 140 mM [K+]in). Compression or illumination cannot elicit obvious changes in mammalian epithelial cell EB1-EGFP patterns. Both Na+ and K+ promote tubulin polymerization in vitro, with 160 mM Na+ as optimal. Different cation sensitivities could be due to sequence divergence or the presence of accessory proteins (MAPs) that obscure cation sensitivity in mammalian MTs. While fundamental MT features (dynamic instability, EB1 plus end tracking) are universal, electrolyte sensitivity and responses could diverge.
evaluation: Claims C175-C181 are supported by citations comparing mammalian and algal systems (Lieuvin et al., 1994; Pohl et al., 2013; Matov et al., 2010; Olmsted and Borisy, 1975; Wolff et al., 1996). The experimental test in mammalian cells (C177) provides direct comparison. The speculation about mechanisms of divergence (C179-C180) is reasonable. The conclusion about universal features versus divergent sensitivities (C181) is well-supported.

result: The pH gradient at pollen tubes may account for MT zone establishment lagging the F-actin, Ca2+, and acid zone at the tip. In sea urchins, a basic shift directs MT-supported processes after fertilization, while depressing pH triggers MT disassembly and inhibits division. An increase of 0.3-0.5 pH unit in mitosis inspired the pH clock hypothesis for cell cycle control. EB1 preferentially binds MT plus ends in mitotic phase extract but uniformly decorates MTs in interphase extract, perhaps analogous to the HA-induced bird cage pattern. Given the central roles of EB1 and dynamic MTs in mitosis and the swiftness of pH-induced changes, tuning pH may control cell cycle in certain organisms.
evaluation: Claims C182-C187 extend the findings to broader biological contexts with citations (Gibbon and Kropf, 1994; Hepler, 2016; Schatten et al., 1985; Gagliardi and Shain, 2013; Tirnauer et al., 2002). While the analogies are interesting and the citations support pH effects in other systems, the speculation about pH controlling cell cycle (C187) goes beyond what is directly demonstrated. The connections are plausible but require further experimental validation in the relevant systems.

result: Absence of most EB1 signals correlates with blocked cell division at 200 mM NaCl. Proliferation of commonly used Chlamydomonas strains is mostly blocked at ≥200 mM NaCl, with adaptation taking months and involving mutation, sexual reproduction, and evolution. The MT system is likely one limiting factor. Proliferation is also partially inhibited at 55 and 100 mM NaCl within 24 hr, though cell division at ~100 mM may be inhibited by additional reactions that may or may not relate to the MT system.
evaluation: Claims C188-C193 are supported by Figure 7 showing correlation between MT dynamics and proliferation, and by citations documenting salt sensitivity (Perrineau et al., 2014; Takouridis et al., 2015; Khona et al., 2016). The inference that MT system is a limiting factor (C191) is reasonable given the correlation, though causation is not definitively proven. The acknowledgment of additional factors at intermediate concentrations (C193) is appropriately cautious.

result: Intracellular acidification followed by immersion in buffers with 5 mM Na+ may mimic natural environmental changes. Acidity and salinity are key factors affecting biota, varying drastically and seasonally in freshwater ecosystems due to climate changes, biogeochemistry, storm surges, snow melts, and anthropogenic activities. pH can decrease by one unit to ~4.5 after downpours. Dissolved organic carbons like HA contribute to local acidification, reaching mM levels. Acidification from past acid rain and projected future atmospheric CO2 increases will shift equilibrium toward permeant neutral acids and favor intracellular acidification.
evaluation: Claims C194-C200 are supported by extensive citations documenting environmental conditions (Sullivan, 2000; Herbert et al., 2015; Feeley et al., 2013; Monteith et al., 2007; Porcal et al., 2009; Zuo et al., 2012; Raven and Caldeira, 2005). The speculation that experimental conditions mimic natural changes (C194) is reasonable given the documented environmental pH and HA levels. This provides important ecological context for the findings.

result: Salinity-dependent effects on Chlamydomonas typify the inverse relationship of salinity and species diversity and the exceptional vulnerability of microalgae and zooplanktons at the bottom of the food chain. The 55 mM Na+ level that perturbs the MT system is readily exceeded in numerous wetlands worldwide from seawater intrusion (~469 mM Na+), saline groundwater, and mining effluents. Deicing road salt is transforming pristine water bodies in North America. At Milwaukee river basin, Cl- exceeded the 24 mM EPA acute criteria in >55% of sites and reached 315 mM.
evaluation: Claims C201-C207 are supported by citations documenting ecological impacts (Herbert et al., 2015; Corsi et al., 2010; Dugan et al., 2017; Jones et al., 2017). The connection between laboratory findings (55 mM Na+ threshold) and environmental conditions is well-established. The specific data about Milwaukee river basin (C206-C207) provides concrete examples of environmental relevance.

result: Current concerns about rising atmospheric CO2 largely center on extracellular acidification and hindered shell formation, but this study suggests concerns should extend to intracellular acidification, rising salinity, and the MT system. Seemingly harmless rises in salinity with chronic mild acidification or temporary acid surges may threaten vulnerable unicellular organisms via perturbed MT systems, reshape aqueous landscapes, and drive evolution.
evaluation: Claims C208-C210 are supported by citations about current concerns (Hoegh-Guldberg et al., 2007; Waldbusser et al., 2013; Fitzer et al., 2016) and by the experimental findings throughout the paper. The suggestion to extend concerns (C209) is justified by the demonstrated sensitivity of the MT system. The speculation about ecological impacts (C210) is reasonable given the documented effects, though long-term consequences require further study.

result: Electrolyte-induced rapid MT changes may be applicable to land plants and particular mammalian cells. Land plant model systems subjected to salt/osmotic/biotic stresses exhibit growth inhibition, MT bundling, and heightened Taxol sensitivity. The similarity comports with common cortical MTs and great homology of non-flagellar MT proteins. MT changes induced by abiotic stresses prompted the proposition that the MT system is an abiotic sensor in plant cells. The EB1-reported scaled responses proportional to [Na+]in and speed of manifestations strengthen the possibility that plant MT system is an upstream player in salinity signaling pathways, if not the sensor itself. Channel-linked MTs are integral to osmolarity signaling in mammalian osmosensory neurons.
evaluation: Claims C211-C216 are supported by extensive citations documenting similar responses in plants (Dhonukshe et al., 2003; Shoji et al., 2006; Wang et al., 2007; Zhang et al., 2012; Fujita et al., 2013; Hardham, 2013; Hashimoto, 2015; Oda, 2015) and the sensor hypothesis (Haswell and Verslues, 2015; Wang et al., 2011a, 2011b). The homology argument (C213) is supported by citations (Dymek et al., 2006; Pedersen et al., 2003; Merchant et al., 2007; Gardiner, 2013). The mammalian example (C216, Prager-Khoutorsky et al., 2014) provides additional support for broader applicability.

result: The study used wild type strain CC-124 and β-tubulin mutant tub2-1 from the Chlamydomonas Resource Center. Cells were cultured in 300 ml pH7.0 TAP liquid media with aeration at 25°C over a 14/10 light/dark cycle until reaching logarithmic phase (5-10×10^6 cells/ml). All experiments were completed at least 2 hr before the dark period. EB1-NG was imaged with Nikon Eclipse widefield microscope with specific equipment. Images were captured as 16-bit grayscale files with 1 s exposure. Streaming videos were recorded for 100 frames at 1 frame/sec.
evaluation: Claims C217-C223 describe standard methods that are clearly stated in the Materials and Methods section. The strains are properly sourced with citations (Bolduc et al., 1988; Lee, 1990; Schibler and Huang, 1991). Culture conditions are standard for Chlamydomonas (Sivadas et al., 2012). Imaging parameters are clearly specified. These methodological details are appropriate and reproducible.
